doc.title: Michael Max Fleming interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, June 8, 2017

chapter: Making his way in New York
title: Moving to New York in 1963 with Curtis Peagler and contacts from Mother's club
summary: He comes to New York with Curtis Peagler's band at Count Basie's club, then moves that fall to a room offered by trumpeter Jerry Ayers. Contacts he made at Mother's club in Cincinnati helped him.

bands.name: Curtis Peagler and the Jazz Disciples

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Talking about the past, you know more than my mother knew about it, man. Come on, man. Okay.
Okay. So you moved to New York and —
Yeah I had a little nest egg.
I had to, that was, you know.
How does a young man find his way in New York City?
Okay how did I get there. Okay. I went to New York in the fall of 1963. Spring of ’63 I came to New York with a local band which was called Curtis Peagler and the Jazz Disciples. Then they recorded.
He was a sax player, wasn’t he?

See you’re good, yeah. That’s when I went with him. We played at Count Basie’s club because Count Basie was managing them at the time. He later went on to play with Count Basie’s band and Ray Charles and different people like that. So I came with that band in the spring. And I made a contact with different people. Made contacts you know. And then that fall a childhood friend of mine who was a trumpet player, his name was Jerry Ayers, he came to his grandmother’s funeral and so he was in town for three or four days. And he said, “If you come to New York you can stay at my place. I’ve got a room for you.” So within a few hours, I broke my mother’s heart I’m sure, I had to get out of there. That was it. And I took whatever my life’s savings was, whatever that was, and said I’m going to make it, do or die. Another background to that, 1963, a few years before that, I was in this club with a guy named DeFelice. He was a drummer. The trumpet player was a guy who played with Duke Ellington, his name was Bill Berry. And there’s another guy who wrote for Woody Herman, his name was Gordon Briscoe. He went to that first high school where I played a tuba. And across the street a woman owned a club called Mother’s, named after the TV show “Mothers,” it was a rainbow club, started bringing in groups from New York. So every group that came in I met them and hung out with the bass players. So then when I got to New York I had contacts. And I met a lot of people, I’m not going to name their names, but I met them. So when I got to New York it wasn’t like who are you, you know. They knew me.
